processing: Lightly oxidised, a touch more than green-style Tieguanyin, ball-rolled and lightly dried; traditionally finished with a light roast. Picked slightly younger than Tieguanyin to keep the aroma.
harvest_season: Spring, about ten days earlier than Tieguanyin (mid to late April), and autumn (late September to October); spring tea is the most prized.
appearance_dry: Small, loosely rolled yellow-green pellets, lighter and thinner than Tieguanyin, with a strong floral smell.
appearance_wet: Thin, soft yellow-green leaves with a faint red edge, smaller than Tieguanyin.
taste_profile: A sharp, sweet floral aroma like osmanthus and gardenia, a light honeyed body, a clean brisk finish and a quicker fade than Tieguanyin.

brewing.notes: Rinse briefly, then short steeps in a porcelain gaiwan with water just off the boil. It gives up its aroma fast and fades after five or six infusions; do not try to stretch it.

vintage_note: Sold by season: spring, when it is the earliest of the Anxi oolongs and is often in the shops by late April, and autumn of the current year. Drink it within the year, sealed and kept cool, because the aroma fades faster than Tieguanyin's; roasted and aged versions exist but are uncommon.
description:
Huang Jin Gui, golden osmanthus, is Anxi's early bird: a yellow-leaved cultivar that sprouts well before Tieguanyin and makes a light, bright oolong with a perfume so sharp that Chinese drinkers call it sky-piercing fragrance. It is cheaper than Tieguanyin and, in spring, often the first new oolong of the year.

The cultivar is Huang Dan, which by two rival legends arose in the middle of the nineteenth century at Huqiu in Anxi county, with mother bushes claimed in both Luoyan and Meizhuang villages; the tea made from it was named for its golden colour and osmanthus-like scent. It has yellowish young leaves, thin and soft, and it is the father of a whole family of modern aromatic hybrids (Jin Guan Yin, Huang Guan Yin, Jin Mu Dan), all of which inherited its nose.

It is made like a green-style Tieguanyin, lightly oxidised and ball-rolled, usually with a slightly younger pick and a light roast or just a careful dry, and it comes out as small, loose, yellow-green pellets. The cup is pale gold, the aroma is osmanthus, gardenia and a little honey, and the taste is light, sweet and brisk, with less body and a shorter finish than Tieguanyin.

Brew it short and hot in a gaiwan and drink the first three steeps for what they are; it is not a ten-infusion tea. It suits mornings and pairs well with light food, and it is a pleasant way to tell which part of an Anxi oolong is aroma and which part is body.

It is sold by season, spring and autumn, and it is a drink-this-year tea, so buy small amounts and keep them sealed and cool. Because it is cheap and fragrant it is also the usual partner in Anxi blends, and a lot of inexpensive Tieguanyin has some Huang Jin Gui in it; sold under its own name it is honest and good value. Next step for the same aroma with more weight: Huang Guan Yin made as Wuyi rock tea.
history:
Huang Jin Gui comes from Huqiu in Anxi county, Fujian, and its origin is told through two legends, both set in the mid-nineteenth century. In one, around 1860, the bride Wang Dan brings seedlings to her wedding with Lin Ziqin, and the tea takes a name close to hers, Huang Dan. In the other, around 1850, the farmer Wei Zhen spots a golden plant beside a brook.

Each story has its own mother bush, one in Luoyan village and one in Meizhuang, which was split off from Luoyan in 1961. The Luoyan bush received a stone tablet in 2009, and its plot became a park in 2017.

The usual account credits the merchant Lin Jintai with making the tea popular in Southeast Asia in the early 1900s and with replacing the old name Huang Dan by Huang Jin Gui. It now counts among Anxi's four famous teas, second to Tieguanyin. In Japan it reached a mass market through Ito En's bottled oolong, launched in 1995.
